text: On the Azure side, Defender for Cloud split posture and detection into two layers. AWS does something structurally similar with two separate services, Security Hub and GuardDuty — and the first thing to get straight is that only one of them actually detects anything.

Security Hub's job is aggregation: it pulls findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, and Config, normalizes every one into the AWS Security Finding Format, and scores your account against standards like the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. GuardDuty is the actual detector, and it doesn't need an agent to do its job — its core detections run against log sources you're already generating, like CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs.

GuardDuty names its findings so you can read them, not decode them. UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce tells you unauthorized access activity against an EC2 instance via SSH brute-forcing. Recon:IAMUser/TorIPCaller flags an IAM user's activity coming from a Tor exit node — worth investigating even before anything is actually accessed. The pattern is always ThreatPurpose, resource type affected, then the threat family — read the name first.

Beyond the default log sources, optional protection plans widen what GuardDuty actually watches: S3 Protection covers S3 data events, EKS Protection reads EKS audit logs, RDS Protection watches login activity, Malware Protection scans EBS volume data, and Lambda Protection covers Lambda network activity. Turn on the plans that match what you actually run — not every plan matters in every account.

In practice: enable GuardDuty in every region you operate in, since threats don't respect your primary-region assumption. Enable Security Hub and turn on the standards your compliance obligations call for. Confirm GuardDuty's findings are actually landing inside Security Hub. And when you're ready to automate response through EventBridge, start with your highest-confidence, highest-severity finding types rather than trying to automate everything at once.

That's the AWS split: GuardDuty detects, Security Hub aggregates and scores. Next lesson moves past detection services entirely into cloud workload protection itself — how Defender for Servers, GuardDuty's malware protection, and their container and serverless equivalents actually defend a VM, a container, and a function differently.
